item.title: “Monks, for direct knowledge of greed, six things should be developed. What six? The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception…
item.description:
“Monks, for direct knowledge of greed, six things should be developed. What six? The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of not-self in suffering, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation. For direct knowledge of greed, monks, these six things should be developed.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.142

item.title: “What leads the world along? What torments itself? And what is the one thing Upon which everything depends?” “Craving leads the world along, Craving torments…
item.description:
“What leads the world along?
What torments itself?
And what is the one thing
Upon which everything depends?”

“Craving leads the world along,
Craving torments itself,
Craving is the one thing
Upon which everything depends.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.63

item.title: “Householder, the form element is the home of consciousness. Consciousness bound by lust for the form element, householder, is called ‘wandering with a home.’ The…
item.description:
“Householder, the form element is the home of consciousness. Consciousness bound by lust for the form element, householder, is called ‘wandering with a home.’ The feeling element is the home of consciousness. Consciousness bound by lust for the feeling element … The perception element … The formation element … The consciousness element is the home of consciousness. Consciousness bound by lust for the consciousness element, householder, is called ‘wandering with a home.’ Thus, householder, is wandering with a home.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.3

item.title: Who has conquered the thorn of sensuality, Insult, injury, bondage, That one stands firm, Like a mountain unshaken — Such a monk, Pleasure and pain…
item.description:
Who has conquered the thorn of sensuality,
Insult, injury, bondage,
That one stands firm,
Like a mountain unshaken —
Such a monk,
Pleasure and pain do not disturb.

From: Udana 3.3

item.title: “Monks, there are these three elements of escape. What three? The escape from sensual pleasures — that is renunciation. The escape from form — that…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three elements of escape. What three? The escape from sensual pleasures — that is renunciation. The escape from form — that is the formless. And as to whatever has come to be, is conditioned, dependently arisen, its escape is its cessation. These, monks, are the three elements of escape.

Knowing the escape from sensual pleasures,
And transcending all forms,
Always ardent, calming all conditioned things —
That monk sees rightly.

From that, being thus liberated,
He perfects direct knowledge,
Dwells at peace, in that very life,
That sage has crossed beyond all yokes.”

From: Itivuttaka 72

item.title: “Monks, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What…
item.description:
“Monks, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What ten? The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of disgust with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of not-self in suffering, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation. These ten perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.56

item.title: “‘The destruction of the cord of continued existence, the destruction of the cord of continued existence,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is the…
item.description:
“‘The destruction of the cord of continued existence, the destruction of the cord of continued existence,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is the cord of continued existence? What is the destruction of the cord of continued existence?” - “Rādha, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, any engagement and clinging, any mental standpoints, attachments, underlying tendencies there are regarding form — that is called the cord of continued existence. Their destruction is the destruction of the cord of continued existence. Regarding feeling … perception … formations … Regarding consciousness, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, any engagement and clinging, any mental standpoints, attachments, underlying tendencies there are — that is called the cord of continued existence. Their destruction is the destruction of the cord of continued existence.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.3

item.title: Elder Nāgasamāla: Adorned, dressed in fine clothes, They set the bait for Death. Then I attended to it, Reflecting wisely — The danger became clear,…
item.description:
Elder Nāgasamāla:

Adorned, dressed in fine clothes,
They set the bait for Death.

Then I attended to it,
Reflecting wisely —
The danger became clear,
I dwelt in disenchantment.

And my mind was liberated.
Seeing the Dhamma as it is,
I attained the three true knowledges,
Accomplishing the Buddha’s teaching.

From: Theragāthā 4.1

item.title: “Aggivessana, what is untrained body and untrained mind? Here, Aggivessana, an untaught ordinary person experiences a pleasant feeling. Having felt that pleasant feeling, he lusts…
item.description:
“Aggivessana, what is untrained body and untrained mind? Here, Aggivessana, an untaught ordinary person experiences a pleasant feeling. Having felt that pleasant feeling, he lusts after it and falls into lust for pleasure. If that pleasant feeling ceases, and due to its cessation, a painful feeling arises, he sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught. Aggivessana, that pleasant feeling arises for him and invades his mind and remains because the body is untrained. That painful feeling arises and invades his mind and remains because the mind is untrained. In this manner, for a person in whom either way — pleasant feeling arises and invades his mind because the body is untrained, and painful feeling arises and invades his mind because the mind is untrained — he is one with untrained body and untrained mind.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 36 – Mahāsaccakasutta

item.title: Elder Mahā-Moggallāna: All conditioned things are impermanent — Having arisen, they must cease. After arising, they cease — Their calming is bliss. Those who see…
item.description:
Elder Mahā-Moggallāna:

All conditioned things are impermanent —
Having arisen, they must cease.
After arising, they cease —
Their calming is bliss.

Those who see the five aggregates
As other, not-self,
Penetrate the subtle,
Like a dart piercing a hair-tip.

Those who see the formations
As other, not-self,
Penetrate the subtle,
Like a dart piercing a hair-tip.

As if struck by a sword,
As if his head were on fire,
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning sensual lust.

As if struck by a sword,
As if his head were on fire,
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning craving for existence.

Not with such weakness,
Not with such little strength,
Can one attain Nibbāna,
Liberation from all bonds.

This young monk,
This supreme man,
Conquering Māra and his army,
Bears this last body.

From: Theragāthā 20.1
